<Rep. Mark Takano>: Committee Democrats appreciated the opportunity to work with Committee Republicans prior to the May 14, 2026, full Committee markup to make technical corrections to the text of H.R. 8052 to improve the policy. Such changes included the provision of a scholarship to attain the certification required by H.R. 8052, as well as a two-year window for current VA staff to obtain such certification, so as to not make this requirement financially restrictive or have it serve as a barrier for an already hard to recruit and hard to retain position.
Despite these changes, Committee Democrats recommend additional amendments to the text to fully ensure that H.R. 8052 meets the needs of the current and future VA sterile processing workforce. For example, during the Subcommittee consideration of this text on March 25, 2026, Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee Members and witnesses discussed the existence of VA's internal certification course, the VA Certified Registered Medical Supply Technician (VA-CRMST) course. This course is designed with VA employees and workloads in mind and was developed to be completed during the workday with no individual expenses by the VA employee.
The text of H.R. 8052 does not include a definition for ``accredited institution'', nor does it delineate which courses must be included in the training program, or the standards it must train to. The text also does not include a reference to the specific accrediting body that would accredit such course or institution. As this text is currently drafted, it is unclear whether the VA-CRMST course is sufficient or if current and future sterile processing technicians must incur costs and obtain a certification through other means. Further, while some associations, like the Healthcare Sterile Processing Association (HPSA), one of the Majority's witnesses for the March 25, 2026, legislative hearing, offers the exam for only $140 after coursework is completed, while some courses offered by other organizations can exceed $5,000 or more.
For most rank-and-file VA sterile processing technicians, the career ladder is GS-3-GS-6. GS-3 is entry level, GS-4 and 5 are developmental levels, and GS-6 is the full performance level. For example, using Cleveland, Ohio, locality pay as the median for VA pay, rank-and-file employees in this occupation earn between $33,867 (GS-3, step 1) and $61,638 (GS-6, step 10). Costs related to required trainings envisioned by this bill could threaten to place current employees in financially precarious situations, especially if they are required to obtain their certification and complete coursework separate from the Department's own free training.
Additionally, while data specific to sterile processing technicians is not readily available in VA's public monthly workforce dashboards, reporting from the VA's Office of the Inspector General indicates that 1 in 4 VA facilities is currently facing a severe occupational staffing shortage within its sterile processing workforce. These numbers very well may be higher today than when they were last reported in August 2025, following the impact of the deferred resignation program, the use of the voluntary early retirement authority, and other attrition. This Committee must focus on the recruitment and retention of this critical workforce, not on adding additional barriers.
Lastly, Committee Democrats would point out that Representative Jen Kiggans' (R-VA) amendment in the nature of a substitute edits establishes this program as a two-year pilot, which would expire in September 2028, in order to save costs. Establishing this sunset date so soon after passage, which may very well occur within the two-year pilot timeframe, may result in additional confusion for current and future VA sterile processing technicians. For example, if a technician is brought on board in July of 2027 and they have two years to obtain their certification, will they still be required to acquire it if this authority expires in September 2028?
Similarly, if one employee hired within the two-year pilot timeframe is required to achieve the certification mandated in H.R. 8052 while another employee that performs the same role, but has joined VA outside of this timeframe does not, how does VA plan to rectify these differences to ensure fairness across its sterile processing technician workforce? VA has been highly concerned by potential inequities between employees performing the same work in other legislative proposals put forth by this Committee; this bill, as currently drafted, potentially opens the Department to additional conflicts and inconsistencies as it pertains to this workforce.
Committee Democrats remain committed to ensuring VA employees have the tools and support they need to provide world-class care to veterans, while rejecting policies that create unnecessary burdens or unfair barriers for the workforce veterans rely on every day.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.
